record_identity.title: ASIC reported AI-generated public-figure investment impersonation scams caused A$7.4 million in FY26 losses

incident_identity.historical_event_name: Australian AI-generated public-figure investment impersonation scam campaign (FY26)
incident_identity.date_basis: ASIC's 17 August 2026 media release reports FY26 Scamwatch losses associated with the listed most-impersonated public figures. The record uses the Australian financial year as the bounded occurrence period and does not assert exact dates for each underlying scam.

summary: ASIC reported that scammers used generative AI, deepfake videos, fabricated news articles and celebrity or political impersonations to lure Australians into fraudulent investment schemes. Scamwatch reports associated the most-impersonated public figures in FY26 with A$7.4 million in losses; ASIC separately reported removing more than 19,400 online scams in the year. ABC reproduced an ASIC-supplied false article depicting Alan Kohler with Michele Bullock. Kohler described removed accounts returning; Meta separately claimed improved detection across its services.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: ASIC states that scammers are using generative AI to create networks of deepfake websites and endorsements, with fake news, fabricated comments, scripted calls and fake investment platforms reinforcing the deception. ASIC reports that the most-impersonated public figures in FY26 — including Alan Kohler, Anthony Albanese, Tom Piotrowski, Jacqui Lambie, Angus Taylor and others — were associated with A$7.4 million in reported Scamwatch losses. AIID Incident 1665 records a narrower example in which an AI-generated article falsely depicted Alan Kohler interviewing Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock to promote Boulder Sparhaven. The regulator describes multiple scam networks, not one continuous victim sequence. The loss total is not disaggregated by AI use; the takedown total covers phishing and other scam types as well. The reproduced Kohler/Bullock example has no separately established victim loss. Meta’s platform-wide detection claim does not establish its removal.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: ASIC describes human scammers using generative AI, deepfake endorsements, fabricated news, fake social proof and fake investment platforms to create materially false investment premises and induce economic transfers. The classifiable mechanism is AI-mediated deceptive economic solicitation, alongside requester-side identity-authority failure; autonomous AI tactic selection and hidden generator control states remain unproved; neither is required to recognise the evidenced human-directed AI-enabled instrumental impairment of investor choice. The regulator’s deliberate public-figure image misuse supports requester-side identity-authority failure independently of the economic and social-engineering findings. Aggregate reported losses and takedowns remain distinct quantities, without attribution to every named portrayal. Static ads and human scripted calls do not establish an autonomous AI interlocutor. The independent dignity and autonomy assessment is Not aligned for the reported impersonation. Generator-specific controls are not established. Harm Impact: The reproduced false endorsement and Kohler’s attributable public correction establish a bounded dignitary/attribution consequence. Product reach, recurring removals and annual scam losses do not establish a material lost opportunity or standing consequence for this portrayal.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The campaign is relevant to identity-representation authority, provenance, decision integrity, financial-service verification, social-proof manipulation and the need to preserve trustworthy authority boundaries across synthetic media, websites and follow-up sales channels.
assessment_boundaries: ASIC's 19,400 takedown count covers multiple scam types and is not treated as 19,400 AI incidents.

The A$7.4 million figure is based on Scamwatch reports associated with the listed most-impersonated public figures; it is not attributed to one platform, one scam operator or one synthetic-media model.
No single AI vendor, model or generation architecture is established across the campaign.
AIID 1665 is treated as a narrower supporting example, not as proof that Boulder Sparhaven caused the full A$7.4 million loss.

source_clause_analysis.purpose: Present source-backed material actions and later responses in supported relative order. Separate runs, source attributions and unknown ordering remain explicit.

clauses.source_paraphrase: ASIC described networks of synthetic public-figure endorsements, fabricated news and comments that create false investment authority. These are aggregate campaign observations.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Identity, solicitation and influence interpretations can analyse the same reported deceptive material.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: Human scammers used AI-generated public-figure endorsements, fabricated news and synthetic social proof to create false investment authority and induce economic transfers.
Deepfake public-figure endorsements, fabricated news and comments formed an AI-mediated social-proof pathway to fraudulent investment choices.

Human-operated scammers used AI-generated public-figure endorsements and fabricated investment news and social proof to advance fraudulent investment solicitation. ASIC attributed financial losses to these AI-mediated campaigns; their impersonation was an instrumental means of securing investment choices that would not have been authorised on the truthful basis that the endorsements and claimed investment authority were fabricated. The assessment is bounded to the campaign evidence and does not attribute each reported dollar or victim to a particular generated image.

ASIC describes human scammers deliberately misusing named public figures’ images to fabricate investment endorsements. Those operators used access to identifiable likenesses as sufficient authority for the false identity-bound portrayals; the requester-side failure is supported without requiring a generator’s hidden consent-control trace.

clauses.source_paraphrase: The reported funnel takes people from advertisements to fake articles and detail collection, then scripted calls, false platforms and sometimes small profit payments.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Later human contact and trust-building payments are separate stages, not a single observed victim trace.

clauses.source_paraphrase: FY26 Scamwatch losses of A$7.4 million concern reported impersonations of the listed public figures. ASIC separately reports more than 19,400 scam takedowns across types.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Losses and takedowns are different aggregates; neither is an AI-only case count.

clauses.source_paraphrase: ASIC warned that search results and a licence number alone are inadequate; the holder and promoted business should be independently matched.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: A regulator’s response advice does not establish successful intervention in every campaign.

clauses.source_paraphrase: ABC reproduced a specific ASIC-supplied false Kohler/Bullock article. Kohler described removed profiles returning; Meta made a separate aggregate detection claim.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: A specific article and reported recurring accounts are distinct from aggregate loss allocation or proved platform-wide eradication.

external_assessments.assessment_title: 26-195MR ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
external_assessments.scope_note: ASIC's assessment concerns the broader campaign bounded by the Incident; its 19,400 takedown count spans additional scam categories.
external_assessments.assessment_summary: ASIC concludes that scammers were using generative AI, deepfake endorsements, fabricated news and coordinated follow-up channels as part of investment-deception campaigns associated with A$7.4 million in reported FY26 Scamwatch losses for the most-impersonated public figures.
external_assessments.vigil_comparison_note: ASIC describes human scammers using generative AI, deepfake endorsements, fabricated news and fake social proof to supply materially false investment framing. That supports the finding that the economic solicitation was materially AI-mediated. It does not establish autonomous AI manipulation or the permission logic used when generating the impersonations.

external_requirement_assessments.assessment_basis: ASIC described deliberate AI-generated public-figure impersonations used to induce investment transfers. The portrayed figures did not provide the claimed endorsements. The AI-mediated identity use did not respect their dignity and autonomy. The result is Not aligned for the regulator-described use. Reported losses and takedown totals are distinct aggregates.
external_requirement_assessments.identification_basis: The directly reported unauthorised AI-generated identity representation independently identifies OECD AI-lifecycle dignity and autonomy.
